structures.overall_structure: α-ferrite matrix without TiB2 (single-phase α-ferrite matrix; the interstitial-free steel reference)

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile test conditions as described in the methods; the IF steel provides the black reference engineering stress-strain curve in Fig. 3(a).

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress-strain curve of the interstitial-free steel (black curve) reported in Fig. 3(a); low, near-flat stress plateau between 300 and 400 MPa extending to ~29% strain.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Values read for the IF steel data points (black stars) in the property maps of Fig. 3(b) and 3(c).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: SANS CMT-3000 testing machine (as described for the quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests in the methods)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Room temperature; nominal strain rate 1×10^-3 s^-1; tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction
characterization_methods.purpose: Obtain the reference engineering stress-strain curve of the interstitial-free steel (black curve in Fig. 3(a))
characterization_methods.key_findings: The IF steel shows the lowest strength among the compared curves (stress plateau between 300 and 400 MPa) but the highest ductility, extending to about 29% strain.

characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize the microstructure of the reference interstitial-free steel
characterization_methods.key_findings: The microstructure of the reference steel is shown in Supplementary Fig. S1 (Fig. S1).

computational_details.simulation_method: Finite element method (FEM) using a two-dimensional representative volume element (RVE)
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Periodic boundary conditions applied to the RVE boundary nodes (edges a, b, c, d; reference points RP-1 and RP-2). The interstitial-free steel is modelled as the α-ferrite matrix without TiB2 (homogeneous α-ferrite / α-ferrite matrix), and its tensile response is predicted using the α-Fe material parameters listed in Table 1.
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: The simulated IF steel true stress-strain response (black curve, Fig. 11(a)) is consistent with the experimentally measured IF steel result, and the same model reproduces the Fe-TiB2 steel response, demonstrating reliability of the FEM approach.

analytical_models.model_name: Flow stress decomposition (σ = σ0 + σgb + σdis)
analytical_models.equation_role: Decompose the matrix flow stress into lattice friction, grain-boundary and dislocation contributions
analytical_models.model_note: Applied to the α-ferrite matrix used to represent the interstitial-free steel.

analytical_models.equation_role: Evolution of dislocation density with plastic strain

unmapped_findings: The chemical composition of the interstitial-free steel reference is given in Table S1 of the Supplementary materials (Supplementary Table S1) and is not reported in the main text.
The microstructure of the interstitial-free steel reference is shown in Fig. S1 of the Supplementary materials (not reproduced in the main text).
Specific modulus (E/ρ) of the IF steel is approximately 26.5 GPa·g⁻¹·cm³, read from the black 'IF steel' star in the property map of Fig. 3(c).
The product of specific yield strength and uniform elongation (SYS × UE) for the IF steel is approximately 5–6 MPa·g⁻¹·cm³, read from the black 'IF steel' star in Fig. 3(c).

A direct comparison between the conventional Fe-TiB2 steel (orange) and interstitial-free steel (black) reference curves reveals that any strength increment due solely to ceramic additions would cause a drastic loss in ductility.
The interstitial-free steel is used as the black tensile reference curve in both Fig. 3(a) and the FE-simulated Fig. 11(a), serving as the α-ferrite matrix benchmark without TiB2.
In the FE simulation the simulated interstitial-free steel curve reaches about 460 MPa at ~0.18 true strain (Fig. 11(a) description).
